sections.title: The SURVIVAL Pattern
sections.text:
Remember the keyword SURVIVAL:
S - Size Up the Situation (Size up your surroundings, your physical condition, and your equipment).
U - Use All Your Senses, Undue Haste Makes Waste (Quick movements without thinking can lead to capture or injury).
R - Remember Where You Are (Always maintain your bearings on a map or mental grid).
V - Vanquish Fear and Panic (Panic is the greatest enemy in a survival crisis).
I - Improvise (Use whatever materials are around you to meet your basic needs).
V - Value Living (Maintain the will to survive above all hardships).
A - Act Like the Natives (Observe how local fauna and indigenous peoples obtain food and water).
L - Live By Your Wits (Learn basic skills before an emergency occurs).

sections.title: Survival Priorities Matrix
sections.text:
The survival hierarchy follows the rule of threes:
1. First Aid — Stop catastrophic bleeding and treat shock immediately.
2. Shelter & Insulation — In harsh weather, exposure can kill in under 3 hours.
3. Fire & Signaling — Provides thermal regulation, water purification, and vector for rescue.
4. Water Procurement — The human body dehydrates rapidly; maximum survival without water is 3 days.
5. Food & Foraging — Caloric depletion occurs over 3 weeks under rest conditions.

sections.title: Site Selection and Hazards
sections.text:
When selecting a shelter site, avoid widow-makers (dead standing trees), flash flood drainages, avalanche chutes, and insect breeding zones.
Locate shelter on dry, elevated ground near a water source and firewood supply.
Ensure good drainage and protect the opening from prevailing winds.

sections.title: Debris Hut Construction
sections.text:
The debris hut is one of the most effective thermal emergency shelters.
1. Place a strong ridgepole (3 to 4 meters long) propped on a sturdy stump or bipod at waist height.
2. Lean rib poles along both sides at a 45-degree angle, leaving a crawl hole opening facing away from wind.
3. Add cross-branch lattice to prevent debris from falling inside.
4. Pile at least 1 meter of dry leaves, needles, brush, and moss over the framework.
5. Fill the interior completely with dry insulation, burrowing in like a sleeping bag.

sections.title: Snow Caves and Quinzhees
sections.text:
In sub-zero alpine conditions, snow provides excellent insulation.
Dig into a deep snowdrift on the leeward side of a ridge.
Shape the roof into a smooth dome to prevent dripping.
Create a sleeping platform higher than the entrance tunnel to trap rising warm air.
Poke a 5 cm ventilation hole in the ceiling for carbon monoxide safety.

sections.title: Locating Natural Water Sources
sections.text:
Water is essential to life. The body loses water through perspiration, respiration, and urination.
Look for signs of water: lush green valley vegetation, swarms of insects, animal trails converging downward, and bird flight paths at dawn and dusk.
In arid regions, dig in outer bends of dry riverbeds where moisture collects beneath the sand.

sections.title: Solar Stills and Transpiration Bags
sections.text:
To construct a belowground solar still:
1. Dig a circular hole 1 meter wide and 60 cm deep.
2. Place a collection container in the center bottom.
3. Place non-poisonous green vegetation around the cup.
4. Cover the pit with clear plastic sheeting, weighting the edges with sand.
5. Place a small stone in the center above the container creating a 45-degree cone.
Solar heat vaporizes ground moisture, condensing on the plastic and dripping into the container.

sections.title: Purification by Boiling and Filtration
sections.text:
Never drink untreated surface water.
1. Boiling: The gold standard. Bring water to a vigorous rolling boil for 1 full minute (3 minutes at elevations over 2,000 meters) to kill all bacteria, cysts, and viruses.
2. Charcoal Sand Filtration: Filter murky water through alternating layers of crushed wood charcoal, clean sand, and fine cloth to remove sediment, tannins, and heavy toxins before boiling.

sections.title: The Fire Triangle and Fuel Preparation
sections.text:
Fire requires heat, fuel, and oxygen. Prepare all fuel stages before lighting a spark:
1. Tinder: Fine, dry fiber that catches sparks (birch bark, cedar shavings, dry cattail down, charred cloth, dry fungus).
2. Kindling: Dry twigs and split pine from pencil lead to thumb thickness.
3. Fuel: Dry hardwoods (oak, hickory, maple, birch) for sustained coals and long-burning heat.

sections.title: Bow Drill and Friction Fire
sections.text:
A bow drill consists of four parts:
1. Spindle: Straight, dry, thumb-thick stick of medium hardness (cedar, yucca, willow).
2. Hearth Board: Flat plank of matching wood with a carved socket and V-notch.
3. Handhold Socket: Hardwood or stone block lubricated with skin oil or green leaf.
4. Bow: Curved branch with cordage wrapped once around the spindle.
Apply steady downward pressure and rapid horizontal strokes until smoking wood dust fills the notch into a glowing ember.

structure.title: Chapter 5: Food Procurement, Traps & Wild Edibles

sections.title: Universal Edibility Test
sections.text:
If forced to test an unknown plant for edibility:
1. Test only one part of one plant at a time.
2. Rub a crushed piece on sensitive skin (inside wrist) and wait 15 minutes for rash or burning.
3. Touch a small portion to the outer lip for 3 minutes.
4. Place on the tongue for 15 minutes without chewing or swallowing.
5. Chew and hold in mouth for 15 minutes.
6. If no burning, bitterness, or nausea occurs, swallow and wait 8 hours drinking only purified water.
Avoid plants with milky sap, almond scent, umbrella-shaped flower clusters, or three-leaf patterns.

sections.title: Figure-4 Deadfall Trap
sections.text:
The Figure-4 deadfall is the premier primitive mechanical trap:
1. Upright stick with a flat bottom and chisel top.
2. Diagonal release stick resting on the upright chisel.
3. Horizontal bait stick notched into the upright and supporting the diagonal.
4. Heavy flat stone or log resting on the diagonal tip.
When an animal perturbs the bait stick, the trigger collapses instantly dropping the stone.

sections.title: Shadow-Tip Direction Finding
sections.text:
1. Plant a straight stick upright in level ground and mark the shadow tip with a peg.
2. Wait 15 to 20 minutes until the shadow moves at least 5 cm.
3. Mark the second shadow tip.
4. Draw a straight line between the two marks: the first mark is always West, the second mark is always East.
5. A perpendicular line indicates true North-South.

sections.title: Mirror and Pyrotechnic Signaling
sections.text:
A flash from a signal mirror can be seen over 50 kilometers in direct sunlight:
1. Hold the mirror in one hand near your eye, aiming the flash at your extended finger.
2. Align your target aircraft or vessel between your sighting finger and the reflection.
3. Sweep the light beam across the horizon to catch the pilot's attention.
Build three fires in a triangle (international distress signal) ready for rapid ignition with dry birch bark.
